I know many persons would have used multiple addresses for their own validators, but it would give us a better idea on the target ratio between validators and EL clients. Possibly stupid question. Why can't the withdrawal-enabling upgrade happen ASAP? Before Shanghai. It requires a hard fork. Since Shanghai is defined as "the hard fork after The Merge", it means the earliest that it could happen is Shanghai by definition. We make the rules, we can change the rules. Probably would be an interesting idea to have ShangHai shipped ASAP with withdrawals only, while also discussing EIPs to include in cancun (for EIPs previously soft committed to shanghai). I'd prefer to see something a bit more - fleshed-out with regard to the motivation here, whether/to what extent there's social consensus around that motivation (not just "avoid vulnerability to censorship by centralized entities", but "avoid vulnerability to censorship by centralized entities by enabling people to en masse withdraw from them and use some another approach" -- the first is a general principle and the second is a specific plan); and - how likely this plan is to achieve said goal, hopefully in a way that's not just handwaving. also, whether certain EIPs actually meaningfully delay Shanghai, for me I can see how, e.g. 4844 is another big chunk to add, but something like PUSH0 is trivial (and already soft-committed to), so it's not clear to me we gain much by removing that form Shanghai There's another aspect here, yes, and 4844 is a good example of it: other Ethereum improvements will also make it easier and less costly for individual stakers to run nodes, and it's not obvious to me that even with that as a goal, the most efficient way to achieve it is to prioritize withdrawals that far above everything else. fwiw I think withdrawals lowers the cost for individual stakers to run nodes substantially - it removes the uncertainty around a potentially large % of their net worth I don't think we should care about staker cost to run nodes. I think we should care about *user* cost to run a node. I think we should care about both Stakers are, by definition, wealthy people. 🙂 They can afford to buy specialized hardware for the task, and there is a pretty high operational expectation of them already. it's not the hardware cost - it's the capital lockup cost They are being compensated, so I don't really care much about the capital lockup cost as long as it doesn't grow so high that the cost of renting attacking power is meaningfully cheapened (which can eventually happen!). What Matt is saying is some people see those costs as too high and hence don't stake So enabling withdrawals might bring in solo stakers who currently are on the sidelines because of that lockup cost That is fine, we have too many stakers already. 🤷 Assuming that's true, there's still value in biasing towards a more diverse group of stakers (who lower the effective rewards by joining and push "incumbent" stakers out) Well they stake, just with LSDs 😄 Sure, I'm not suggesting that we *never* implement withdraws. I just don't think there is significant urgency. I think there are other things that are far more critical to the longe term health of Ethereum than stakers being able to withdraw in 2023 rather than 2024. I think when removing withdrawals from the scope of The Merge, we already sort of reneged on a commitment we had made to stakers about when they could expect to withdraw their stake, and personally feel we've very much committed to enable this ASAP after it. that said, I'm fine with "ASAP" meaning "in the next fork, which may not include _only_ withdrawals" rather than "we put everything on hold and focus on withdrawals exclusively" if, like Greg was saying, there are security/testing/complexity reasons to do _just_ withdrawals, that's fine, but to me the "level of urgency" is "we bundle this in the next available upgrade" rather than "we change our upgrade process to ship this ASAP" I strongly disagree with this. I have been thinking more on this to figure out why it bothers me so much. I think the reason it bothers me so much is because we (core devs as a group) have not come to any consensus on releasing withdraws in the HF after the merge. It has been discussed a bit and certainly some people want it, but discussion for "post merge HF planning" was shutdown many many months ago, prior to any actual consensus that I remember. Some people (I don't know who or how many) have been publicly telling people that withdraws will happen in the hard fork after The Merge despite there being no consensus on that fact nor even the opportunity to discuss it. Now we are opening up discussion and using the argument "well, we already promised people", but those promises were made by individuals without any sort of consensus. This rubs me in a very wrong way because it feels like a mechanism for subverting governance (whether intentional or not this time around). If people with a large social reach can just assert publicly what will be in the next HF without any actual discussion, and then use the argument during consensus making that "we already promised people this will be in the next HF" it is a huge attack vector against our consensus based governance process. https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/blob/dev/specs/capella/beacon-chain.md#withdrawal ? > we (core devs as a group) have not come to any consensus on releasing withdraws in the HF after the merge The EL withdrawal EIP is also CFI'd https://github.com/ethereum/execution-specs/blob/master/network-upgrades/mainnet-upgrades/shanghai.md IIRC part of the reason to _stop_ discussing Shanghai further was that we still very far from it and had already CFI'd two large EIPs (withdrawals + EOF) and several small ones again, we can reconsider these decisions, sure, but I think it's very much the case that there was some soft commitment on the EL and CL side that withdrawals were/are high priority post merge > If people with a large social reach can just assert publicly what will be in the next HF without any actual discussion, and then use the argument during consensus making that "we already promised people this will be in the next HF" it is a huge attack vector against our consensus based governance process. excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
I have been thinking more on this to figure out why it bothers me so much.  I think the reason it bothers me so much is because we (core devs as a group) have not come to any consensus on releasing withdraws in the HF after the merge.  It has been discussed a bit and certainly some people want it, but discussion for "post merge HF planning" was shutdown many many months ago, prior to any actual consensus that I remember.  Some people (I don't know who or how many) have been publicly telling people that withdraws will happen in the hard fork after The Merge despite there being no consensus on that fact nor even the opportunity to discuss it.  Now we are opening up discussion and using the argument "well, we already promised people", but those promises were made by individuals without any sort of consensus.

This rubs me in a very wrong way because it feels like a mechanism for subverting governance (whether intentional or not this time around).  If people with a large social reach can just assert publicly what will be in the next HF without any actual discussion, and then use the argument during consensus making that "we already promised people this will be in the next HF" it is a huge attack vector against our consensus based governance process.

What *really* bothers me is that those people are now claiming "but we made promises to users" when lobbying for withdraw inclusion in Shanghai.  If we allow that as a valid argument in Shanghai planning, it teaches people that the way to get your thing included in a hard fork is to just start promising it to users without buy-in/agreement from the broader group.

The only thing withdraws do for *users* (the people we are building for) is increase the amount of security we get at the current ROI schedule.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus

Maybe it still makes Shanghai because it is easy to implement, but I don't think that can be known until we have seen what it is competing against.
